name: Thomas Jefferson
role: Principal author of the Declaration of Independence; third President of the United States (1801-1809)
summary: A Virginia planter and republican theorist who argued that government rests on the consent of the governed, should be limited, divided among separate branches and kept close to the people through states and local wards. He championed religious freedom and a wall between church and state, preferred an agrarian society of small landholders to banks and manufactures, and doubted that one generation may bind another. He enslaved people throughout his life, called slavery a moral evil, and wrote that Black people were probably inferior and should be freed and colonised elsewhere.

property-fundamental.rationale: Second inaugural speaks of the state of property, equal or unequal, that results from each person's industry or that of his fathers, and the national-bank opinion defends state property laws; but the 1789 letter to Madison says legislatures may change descent, entails and perpetual appropriations, and he abolished entail and primogeniture.

strong-leader.rationale: Notes on Virginia calls concentrating government powers in one body the definition of despotism and wants powers divided so none can exceed its limits; the first inaugural asks for the supremacy of civil over military authority and a government of restrained power.

state-harmful.rationale: First inaugural calls a wise and frugal government necessary to complete the people's happiness and calls for preserving the general government in its whole constitutional vigor as the sheet anchor of peace and safety.

empower-police-military.rationale: As president he reduced military forces and expenditure and shrank the Navy to local-defence gunboats; his first inaugural lists economy in public expense among his principles.

decide-locally.rationale: First inaugural lists support of the state governments in all their rights as the most competent administrations for domestic concerns; his ward-republic plan gave small wards the care of poor, roads, police and small justice, because these were better managed near at hand.

more-religion-public.rationale: Second inaugural: he never prescribed religious exercises for the nation, leaving them to the churches; the Statute says no one may be compelled to support any religious worship or ministry.

gradual-change.rationale: Letter to Madison (1789): no society can make a perpetual constitution or law, and the earth belongs to the living; Smith letter: a rebellion every generation or so is healthy.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Notes on Virginia doubts the wisdom of inviting immigrants by extraordinary encouragements, fearing monarchical principles, but says those who come of themselves are entitled to all the rights of citizenship; he welcomed skilled artisans.

free-trade.rationale: The 1774 Summary View claims free trade with all parts of the world as a natural right of the colonists, and the first inaugural wants commerce with all nations; but he signed the 1807 Embargo Act and wrote that workshops should remain in Europe. The evidence points both ways.

revolution-justified.rationale: Drafted the Declaration of Independence; in 1787 wrote that he hoped the country would never be twenty years without such a rebellion as Shays's, so that rulers are warned that people keep the spirit of resistance.

experts-over-public.rationale: Notes on Virginia: every government degenerates when trusted to the rulers alone, and the people themselves are its only safe depositories; Adams letter: leave the citizens the free election of the aristoi.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Wrote that those who labour in the earth are God's chosen people and that every citizen should be employed in improving the land; as legislator he drafted the laws abolishing entail and primogeniture and dividing intestate land equally, which he said laid the axe to the root of pseudo-aristocracy.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Argued in 1791 that Congress had no constitutional power to charter a national bank; according to Wikipedia he later called the bank deadly hostile to republican government and wanted it to lapse in 1811. This does not state a view on abolishing central banking or leaving money to the market.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Declaration charges George III with a history of injuries establishing tyranny; letter to Adams says rank, birth and tinsel-aristocracy will shrink into insignificance.

democracy-best.rationale: First inaugural calls absolute acquiescence in the decisions of the majority the vital principle of republics, while insisting the majority's will be reasonable and respect minority rights; he expected citizens generally to elect the good and wise.

natural-rulers.rationale: Letter to John Adams (1813): there is a natural aristocracy among men grounded in virtue and talents, the most precious gift of nature for the instruction, trusts and government of society.

political-violence-never.rationale: Drafted the Declaration justifying armed separation, and in 1787 defended rebellion and wrote that the tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time.

war-builds-character.rationale: Second inaugural: war is a suspension of useful works and peace a return to progress; he held that a just nation's word and sound interests are better than recourse to armaments.

separate-church-state.rationale: Danbury Baptists letter (1802): the First Amendment builds a wall of separation between church and state; he drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, passed 1786.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Notes on Virginia attacks heresy and blasphemy laws and says the government's powers reach only acts injurious to others; the Statute disconnects civil capacities from religious opinions.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: He recognised that Native peoples held a right of soil that had to be bought by treaty, but his 1803 letter to Harrison and second inaugural describe a policy of drawing tribes to agriculture so they will cede land, and extinguishing the native right of soil.

taxation-theft.rationale: Declaration complains of taxes imposed without consent, which implies taxes imposed with consent are legitimate; second inaugural describes taxes funding government and paying the debt.

harm-principle.rationale: Notes on Virginia: the legitimate powers of government extend to such acts only as are injurious to others, with the example of a neighbour's belief that there are twenty gods or none; stated for religion, and the same revised code he helped prepare made sodomy a punishable crime.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Notes on Virginia: he advances as a suspicion, to be hazarded with great diffidence, that Black people are inferior to whites in endowments of body and mind, and says it is nature, not condition, that produced the distinction; he also noted that more observation was needed.

territorial-expansion.rationale: As president he made the Louisiana Purchase (doubling the country's size), and the second inaugural endorses extending the limits of the Union and extinguishing native rights of soil.

universal-morality.rationale: Declaration treats the equality and unalienable rights of all men as self-evident truths; Notes appeals to reason and free inquiry as the means of finding truth.

national-self-determination.rationale: Declaration: one people may dissolve the political bands that connected them with another and assume a separate and equal station.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Notes on Virginia: reason and free inquiry are the only effectual agents against error, and reason and persuasion the only practicable instruments for truth in religion.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Inferred: Notes on Virginia fears that immigrants from absolute monarchies will bring and pass on foreign principles and language that make government heterogeneous, so he wants the country harmonious in what it must do together.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Notes on Virginia warns that rulers will become corrupt and that corruption will seize the heads of government, spread to the people, and that rulers readily make interested use of power.

night-watchman-state.rationale: First inaugural defines good government as one that restrains men from injuring one another and otherwise leaves them free to pursue their own industry; but he also proposed public schools and later wished a constitutional amendment for federal spending on roads, canals and education.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Notes on Virginia: freed slaves should be removed beyond the reach of mixture, which would stain the blood of the master, and it is better to keep the races as distinct as nature formed them.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Declaration says all men are created equal and the first inaugural calls for equal and exact justice to all men, but he held slaves all his life and wrote in Notes on Virginia a suspicion that Black people are inferior in body and mind, while also holding that they have natural rights. His draft Declaration condemned the slave trade as a cruel war against human nature, and in 1820 he wrote that emancipation and expatriation would be worth great sacrifice but that we have the wolf by the ear.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Statute for Religious Freedom: all men shall be free to profess and maintain their religious opinions by argument; Notes holds that coercion of opinion only makes hypocrites and that free inquiry should be indulged.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Plan for Virginia's local schools in Notes on Virginia: instead of giving children the Bible and Testament at an age too young for religious inquiry, teach history and morality.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Declaration: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

population-transfer.rationale: Notes on Virginia proposes that freed slaves be colonised elsewhere, and his private letters from 1803 increasingly support removing Native tribes west of the Mississippi.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: First inaugural says those who wish to dissolve the Union or change its republican form should be left undisturbed, because error of opinion can be tolerated where reason is free to combat it.

separated-powers.rationale: Notes on Virginia: all powers of government resulting to the legislature is the definition of despotism; government should be divided and balanced among several bodies so none can transcend its limits.

party-controls-media.rationale: Second inaugural: freedom of discussion unaided by power is sufficient for protecting truth, and the press, confined to truth, needs no other legal restraint than state laws against falsehood.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: First inaugural: peace, commerce and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none.

people-in-arms.rationale: First inaugural calls a well-disciplined militia the best reliance in peace and for the first moments of war until regulars can relieve them, so he did not call for abolishing professional forces; he did hold regulars to be subordinate to civil authority.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Notes on Virginia: those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God; the mobs of great cities add to pure government what sores add to the body.

death-penalty.rationale: The revised criminal code reported in Notes on Virginia keeps death for treason and murder while replacing it with hard labour for lesser crimes.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Notes on Virginia: the remedy for Virginia's defects is a convention to fix the constitution, amend its defects and bind the branches of government.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Notes on Virginia approves suspending clergy salaries by law, and his 1789 letter says a nation may change the appropriation of lands given to the church in perpetuity; he did not call for placing clergy under civil authority as such.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Declaration: the King is charged with tyranny and treated as accountable to the people; Summary View says rights are derived from natural law, not the gift of the chief magistrate.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Summary View and Declaration hold the King's acts accountable to law and the people's rights; Notes calls elective despotism not the government sought.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Revised criminal code reported in Notes on Virginia lists apostasy and heresy as offences to be pitied, not punished; Notes also attacks the existing penalties for denying the Trinity.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Drafted Virginia's laws abolishing entails and primogeniture, calling them the axe laid to the root of pseudo-aristocracy; wrote to Madison that hereditary orders, distinctions and offices cannot bind a later generation; first inaugural asks honour to come from actions, not birth.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Notes on Virginia lists as a defect that the ordinary legislature can alter the constitution and proposes a convention to fix it, so that acts violating it become nullities; says essential rights should be fixed on a legal basis while rulers are honest. His 1789 letter to Madison also holds that no constitution should be perpetual.

elective-rulers.rationale: Declaration condemns the King's rule; the Adams letter and Notes favour choosing officers by election of the citizens, and first inaugural says honour should come from actions, not birth.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Declaration says that when a government becomes destructive of the people's rights they may alter or abolish it, and lists the King's violations; the Summary View charges the King with deviating from the line of duty.

military-guardian-role.rationale: First inaugural lists the supremacy of the civil over the military authority among the essential principles of government.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Declaration lists imposing taxes without the colonists' consent among the King's injuries; Summary View protests taxation without representation.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The revised criminal code he helped draft (reported in Notes on Virginia) lists sodomy among crimes punished by dismemberment; his later view is not recorded.

suppress-opposition.rationale: First inaugural: those who would dissolve the Union or change its form should stand undisturbed, as monuments of the safety with which error of opinion may be tolerated; the Kentucky Resolutions protest the Sedition Act.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Notes on Virginia: it does him no injury for a neighbour to say there are twenty gods or none, and heresy laws should go; revised code proposed that apostasy and heresy be pitied, not punished.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Summary View (1774) objected to Britain's restrictions on colonial trade and its laws made by a body foreign to the colonies, claiming a natural right of free trade.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Letter to Adams: proposed dividing counties into wards, little republics with small-scale self-government over poor-relief, roads, police and elections, with ward-meetings able to give the genuine sense of the people.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Declaration: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, even though rights are endowed by a Creator.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: First inaugural states his principle of peace, commerce and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; his policy in 1807 to Britain and France was the Embargo.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Letter to Adams criticises hereditary succession to office as a product of an alliance of church and state and says rank and birth are falling into contempt; Notes also describes hereditary wisdom as a false premise.

property-franchise.rationale: Notes on Virginia criticises the freeholder requirement because most men who pay taxes and fight are unrepresented, and says suffrage should be extended to such numbers as defy corruption, though he did not propose universal suffrage.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Letter to Adams: describes the great accumulations of wealth in families under entail as the basis of a pseudo-aristocracy that his abolition laws aimed to dismantle; says an artificial aristocracy of wealth and birth is distinct from the natural one.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: from his stated view that government has no authority over opinion, and that coercing opinion only makes hypocrites, he would oppose the state promoting any belief, atheism included.

second-chamber.rationale: Notes on Virginia criticises Virginia's senate for being chosen like the lower house, saying different houses should bring in different interests or principles; he treats a second chamber as useful when properly composed.

free-public-college.rationale: Notes on Virginia sets out a plan for public education in which selected poor boys are schooled and sent to the college at public expense, while others pay; it is not universal free tuition.

arms-reduction.rationale: As president he reduced military forces and spending, incorporated cheap gunboats for local defence and cut the Navy; first inaugural puts economy in public expense among his principles.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Proposed to Madison (1789) that a constitution declare no government can validly contract debt it cannot pay within 19 years, with later contracts void after that term; second inaugural aims to pay for wars within the year without burdening future generations.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Letter to Adams: the Virginia law he drafted divided intestate lands equally among all children or other representatives, replacing primogeniture.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Statute he drafted disestablished the Church of England in Virginia and gave all faiths equal civil standing; Notes praises states with no establishment and says no two states have established the same religion.

race-social-construct.rationale: Notes on Virginia says the difference of colour between races is fixed in nature and real, and speaks of keeping the races as distinct as nature has formed them.

national-church-status.rationale: Drafted the Virginia Statute disestablishing the state church and, in Notes on Virginia, praised Pennsylvania and New York for thriving without any establishment.

self-ownership.rationale: Cited in Wikipedia: as a lawyer in 1770 he argued that everyone comes into the world with a right to his own person and may use it at his own will; this was advocacy for a client, and he enslaved people himself.

no-business-privileges.rationale: His 1791 bank opinion objected that incorporating a bank would override state laws against mortmain and monopoly; his 1789 letter to Madison denies that a legislature can grant perpetual monopolies in commerce, the arts or sciences.

notes: His words and acts conflict on slavery and equality, so those answers are mixed. On race, the Notes state a suspicion of Black inferiority, hedged as a suspicion only; no later retraction was found in the sources read. On free trade the sources point both ways (1774 free-trade claim, Notes against home manufactures, 1807 Embargo). The Kentucky text used is the 1799 resolution; Jefferson drafted the 1798 original. Founders Online was unreachable, so the 1787 Smith letter is read through a quoting article. The Virginia Statute text is read through Wikipedia. Not reached: letters to Peter Carr, Kercheval, McPherson, Austin and Burwell, and his Annual Messages.
